title: I am Brahman
hookLine: an ancient text says the gods would rather you didn't find out who you are
carry: aham brahmasmi: your deepest self is the ultimate reality
tomorrow: karma: the crane, the wife and the butcher

lines: THE GODS WOULD RATHER YOU DIDN'T KNOW.
cards: A herd of cows. They give milk, they pull the cart, they are a family's living. Suppose one wanders off one day, free.
For the owner, losing even one is a nuisance, and losing many is worse. Here's the strange part. An Upanishad says the gods see people that way.
It's not pleasing to the gods, it says, that people should come to know this. Know what? Three words.

teach.h: IN THE BEGINNING, BRAHMAN KNEW ITSELF.
teach.b: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad tells it like a creation story. In the beginning, this world was Brahman, the ultimate reality. And it knew itself, saying: aham brahmasmi.
I am Brahman. By knowing that, it became everything. Whoever awakens to this, the text says, among the gods, the sages or people, becomes that.
Even now, whoever knows I am Brahman becomes all this, and even the gods can't stop them, because that person has become the gods' own Self.

But someone who worships a god thinking, he is one and I am another, doesn't know, the text says. Then the cow line: just as many cows serve a person, each person serves the gods, and losing even one cow is unpleasant.
So the gods aren't pleased when people learn this. A startling, almost funny picture: whoever knows this can't be held back, not even by the gods.
Aham brahmasmi is one of the four great sayings, the mahavakyas, beside the tat tvam asi you met with the salt and the seed.

teach.h: YOU ARE THAT, THEN: I AM.
teach.b: Tat tvam asi is the teacher saying: you are that.
Aham brahmasmi is the student finally saying it from the inside: I am. Different schools hear it differently. Advaita hears strict identity.
Ramanuja's and Madhva's followers read the same line within their own views, where the soul stays distinct and devotion stays whole. And notice what it isn't.
On a yoga playlist, aham brahmasmi can sound like the ego saying I'm God. Teachers say it's the opposite: the small self with its labels steps aside, and what's left, your deepest self, is Brahman.

how: Aham brahmasmi is one of the four mahavakyas, the great sayings, traditionally associated with the four Vedas and taught to renunciants in some Advaita orders; students of Vedanta meditate on it, each school reading it in its own way.

o: a fate the gods hand out to each person
action, even the act of knowing who you are
the duty to serve the gods, like cattle

games.q: I am Brahman — tap the pairs.
p: aren't pleased when people know this

s: the Brihadaranyaka says the gods are glad when people learn who they are
it says the gods aren't pleased, the way an owner doesn't like losing cows.
aham brahmasmi and tat tvam asi are both counted among the great sayings
they're two of the four mahavakyas.
every Hindu school reads 'I am Brahman' as strict identity
Advaita does; Ramanuja's and Madhva's followers read it within their own views.

games.q: you're a god in the Upanishad, and humans are starting to realize 'I am Brahman'. how do you feel, according to the text?
o: not pleased: it's like losing cows.
games.why: the text says it isn't pleasing to the gods that people should know this, because each one who knows is free.

practice: Say the word I silently, once, and notice where it seems to come from: not your name, not your job, not your story, just the plain sense of I am, here, now.
Rest in that, and let every label fall away for a breath; if one comes back, that's fine, notice it and return to the simple sense of being.
You don't have to believe anything, just look, and if you pray, you can rest in God as the ground of that I.

wordCard.voice: Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. On the jnana road the action is knowing, and in the Upanishad, whoever knows I am Brahman can't be held back, even by the gods.

orig.note: Sanskrit: aham, I + brahma, Brahman + asmi, am. Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.10.

carryVoice: Your line: aham brahmasmi, your deepest self is the ultimate reality. No label needed for that one. Day three hundred thirteen, done.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.10 (the gods not pleased; people like cattle to the gods)
